latest_nl_proof:
Let m = |X| and n = |Y|. For each integer r >= 0, write [r] = {1,2,...,r}, with [0] = the empty set. Since X and Y are finite, there exist bijections a : X -> [m] and b : Y -> [n]. If f : X -> Y is injective, then g := b o f o a^{-1} : [m] -> [n] is also injective. Thus it is enough to prove the following claim:

Claim. If there exists an injective map [m] -> [n], then m <= n.

We prove the claim by induction on n.

Base case n = 0. Then [n] is empty. A function [m] -> empty set can exist only if [m] is empty, so m = 0. Hence m <= 0 = n.

Inductive step. Assume the claim holds for some n >= 0, and let g : [m] -> [n+1] be injective. If m = 0, then m <= n+1 is immediate. So suppose m >= 1.

Let k = g(m). Define tau : [n+1] -> [n+1] to be the transposition that swaps k and n+1 and fixes every other element. Then h := tau o g is injective, and h(m) = n+1.

Now let i be any element of [m-1]. If h(i) = n+1, then h(i) = h(m), contradicting injectivity of h. Therefore h(i) is in [n] for every i in [m-1]. So the restriction of h to [m-1] is an injective map [m-1] -> [n]. By the induction hypothesis, m-1 <= n. Hence m <= n+1.

This proves the claim.

Applying the claim to the injective map g gives m <= n, that is, |X| <= |Y|. Therefore, if there exists an injective function f : X -> Y between finite sets, then |X| <= |Y|.
